title: A Simple Script for Hard Feedback Conversations
summary: Hard feedback goes better with a script: write down what you saw and its impact, ask for their side, agree on one visible change, then follow up when it works.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
A pull request has gone three rounds longer than anyone expected. Somewhere in round two the comments got sharp, and by the end of the afternoon two of your teammates have stopped talking to each other. You're the lead. Everyone can see that somebody needs to say something. The hard part is saying it so the next review gets easier and doesn't get worse.

Hard feedback is hard because two things are true at once. The work needs the truth, and the person needs to keep their dignity. Protect only comfort and the behavior repeats. Protect only being right and trust takes the hit. Kim Scott's Radical Candor squeezes this into one line: care personally and challenge directly at the same time. Caring without challenging is what she calls ruinous empathy, where you stay silent or sugar-coat. Challenging without caring is obnoxious aggression.

A script helps because it gives the conversation a path before emotions draw their own map. This one has four steps (prepare, open, listen, agree) plus a fifth that happens later.

Write it down before you talk

Most of the work happens before the meeting. The Center for Creative Leadership's SBI model makes a good template: name the Situation, describe the Behavior you actually observed, then the Impact it had (CCL). Their own example: say "You interrupted me while I was telling the team about the monthly budget," and skip "You were rude." The first is something you both saw. The second is a verdict on a person.

On an engineering team, it might look like this:

  • Situation: "In yesterday's review of the billing migration PR..."
  • Behavior: "...the migration note had no rollback path, and two replies to the reviewer's questions said 'just read the code.'"
  • Impact: "The reviewer couldn't judge the release risk, the PR went three more rounds and the release slipped a day."

Then add the piece SBI leaves open: what you'd like to happen next time. "Every migration PR gets a rollback section in its description" is something a person can start doing on Monday.

Why be this precise? In 1996, Avraham Kluger and Angelo DeNisi pulled together 607 effect sizes from feedback studies. On average, feedback improved performance, yet in over a third of cases it made performance worse. Their explanation is that feedback backfires when it pulls attention off the task and onto the self (summary of Kluger and DeNisi, 1996). "You're careless" sends attention straight to the self. "The note had no rollback path" keeps it on the work, where something can actually be fixed.

A shape you can borrow

Here's what I saw. Here's what it caused. What was going on from your side? Next time, here's the one thing I'd like us to change.

Open with the topic and the reason

Start plainly: "I want to talk about yesterday's review, because I think we can make the next one smoother." That names the topic and your intention in one breath. It doesn't pretend nothing happened, and it doesn't open with a verdict.

They may still feel uncomfortable, and that's normal. Kind feedback can still sting. What makes it kind is that the sting comes with a fair purpose they can see.

Ask for their side, and mean it

After the behavior and the impact, stop and ask: "What was happening on your end?" CCL calls this extra step intent. You ask what the person was trying to do, and one-way feedback becomes a two-way conversation. Maybe a deadline was squeezing them. Maybe the requirement changed in a side chat nobody shared. Maybe nobody ever told them the team expects rollback notes.

Context doesn't erase the impact, but it changes the fix. A skill gap needs teaching. A priority conflict needs a talk with whoever set the deadline. Two people who've stopped trusting each other need to sit down together. Same symptom, three very different next steps.

If it gets defensive, lower the stakes

Feedback isn't a courtroom, and you aren't there to win. If the other person gets defensive, repeating the evidence louder rarely helps. Bring the scope back down: "I'm not questioning your intentions. I'm talking about the effect this had on the review." That line separates the person from the behavior, so they can listen without feeling their whole self is on trial.

If it's still too heated, pause. "Let's pick this up tomorrow morning" is a perfectly good sentence. Pushing on while one person is flooded mostly creates things you'll both have to repair later.

Close with one visible change

End on something you'll both be able to see. For example:

  • The next large PR includes a short risk and rollback section.
  • When a review thread passes three back-and-forths, it moves to a quick call.
  • The next estimate lists its assumptions.
  • The next handoff names the owner, the status and the open questions.

Without a concrete next behavior, the conversation tends to end as emotional cleanup, and the way the work gets done stays exactly the same.

Follow up, especially when it worked

The follow-up matters more than perfect wording. If they adjust, say so, and be specific: "The rollback section on the payments PR saved the reviewer a lot of digging." If the old pattern comes back, return to the specific behavior instead of restarting from frustration. People take hard feedback much better when the standard is the same every week and nobody is trying to embarrass them.

For a wider toolkit, including feedback to peers and to your own manager, read giving and receiving feedback as an engineer. For the smaller, everyday kind, see giving constructive feedback.

Before your next hard conversation, write the three lines (situation, behavior, impact) plus the one change you're asking for on a sticky note. If you can't fill in the behavior line with something you actually saw, you're not ready to have the talk yet.

faqs.q: How do I give difficult feedback to a coworker?
faqs.a: Prepare three things first: the situation, the behavior you actually observed and its impact. Open by naming the topic and why you're raising it, ask for their side, then agree on one specific change you'll both be able to see. Follow up later, especially if they improved.

faqs.q: What is the SBI feedback model?
faqs.a: SBI comes from the Center for Creative Leadership: describe the Situation, the observable Behavior and its Impact. CCL suggests a fourth step, asking about the person's intent, so the feedback turns into a two-way conversation.

faqs.q: What should I do if someone gets defensive during feedback?
faqs.a: Lower the stakes instead of repeating the evidence louder. Say clearly that you're talking about the effect of one behavior and that you aren't judging their intentions or character. If emotions are running too high, pause and continue the next day.

Yes. Kluger and DeNisi's 1996 meta-analysis found that feedback helps on average, but in over a third of cases it made performance worse, especially when it pushed attention off the task and onto the person's sense of self. Keep feedback on specific, observable work.
